---
title: "The mean structure"
---

This is the first of seven chapters that open the native engine and show every
matrix it works with. The chapters, in order:

1. **The mean structure** (this chapter): the RAM form, the implied means,
   the discrepancy and its gradient, and the moment count.
2. [Scale and conditioning](02-scale.qmd): why the engine fits in
   centered coordinates and when it may shift the data.
3. [Constrained estimation](03-constraints.qmd): constraint rows,
   the solver, the acceptance gate and the Newton polish.
4. [Fixed exogenous variables](04-fixed-x.qmd): `fixed_x`, the
   conditional likelihood and the comparison refusals.
5. [Inference](05-inference.qmd): information, the sandwich, MBCO
   and `anova()`.
6. [The product term](06-product-term.qmd): `x:m`, its column,
   why the paths are least squares, rules 8 and 9 and the model test.
7. [The four-way decomposition](07-four-way.qmd): CDE, INTref,
   INTmed and PIE derived, with their delta-method standard errors.

Each chapter fits real models to the bundled `mediation_demo` data, prints the
matrices the engine builds, derives the formulas that produce them, and checks
the numbers against lavaan and OpenMx. Each chapter runs on its own.

| | |
|---|---|
| **You need** | medfit 0.9.0 or later; matrix algebra and the normal likelihood at the level of a first course in multivariate statistics |
| **You get** | the RAM matrices of a fitted model, the implied mean and covariance computed by hand, the discrepancy and its gradient derived and checked, and the moment and degrees-of-freedom count |
| **Time** | about 40 minutes |

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(medfit)
# These chapters teach the joint likelihood and the covariance-first form of the engine, so every fit pins the
# 0.14.x settings. medfit 0.15.0 itself defaults to fixed_x = the exogenous variables and meanstructure = TRUE; the
# note at the end of chapter 1 and Section 6 of chapter 4 show what that changes. Pass an explicit value to a call to override the pin.
fit_sem <- function(model, data, ..., fixed_x = FALSE, meanstructure = NULL) {
  medfit::fit_sem(model, data, ..., fixed_x = fixed_x, meanstructure = meanstructure)
}
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
f4 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 4)
mx <- function(x, d = 4) round(x, d)
```

## 1. The model

We use the smallest mediation model: a treatment, one mediator and an outcome.
Two lines of syntax write the paths, and two more write the intercepts. An
**intercept statement** (`y ~ 1`) turns on the mean structure: the model then
describes the means of the observed variables as well as their covariances. (Since 0.15.0 the
mean structure is on by default; this chapter pins the earlier default, where only an intercept statement or a
product term turns it on, so the step from covariances to means is visible.)
Every observed intercept the text does not write is added and left free, so one
intercept line would be enough; the second only makes the model explicit.

```{r}
#| label: model
syntax <- "
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment
  mediator1 ~ 1
  outcome ~ 1
"
fit <- fit_sem(syntax, mediation_demo)
ram <- fit@internals$ram
theta <- fit@theta
n <- fit@n_obs
round(theta, 4)
```

`theta` is the **parameter vector**: the free parameters in the order the engine
keeps them. There are `r length(theta)` of them: three paths, three variances and three intercepts.
`treatment` is **exogenous**: no path in the model points to it, so its own mean and
variance are parameters, and its "intercept" is its mean. The
engine also keeps the model as a **RAM specification** (`fit@internals$ram`),
which the next section opens.

## 2. The RAM form: A, S, F and m

RAM stands for reticular action model. It writes every structural equation
model with four matrices. Put all the variables of the model, observed and latent,
in one vector $v$ of length $n_v$. Then the model says

$$
v = A\,v + m + e, \qquad \operatorname{E}(e) = 0, \quad \operatorname{Cov}(e) = S_{\text{ram}} .
$$

The pieces are:

- $A$, the **path matrix** ($n_v \times n_v$). Entry $A_{r c}$ is the effect of
  variable $c$ on variable $r$: a one-headed arrow from $c$ to $r$.
- $m$, the **intercept vector** (length $n_v$). Entry $m_r$ is the intercept of
  variable $r$'s equation. An exogenous variable's equation is just its mean, so
  its intercept is its mean.
- $S_{\text{ram}}$, the **covariance matrix of the errors** ($n_v \times n_v$).
  Its diagonal holds the residual variances (or, for an exogenous variable,
  its variance); an off-diagonal entry is a two-headed arrow.
- $F$, the **selection matrix** ($p \times n_v$, with $p$ the number of observed
  variables). Each row has one 1 and picks one observed variable out of $v$.

We read the real matrices of our fit. The helper `.sem_ram_mats()` builds $A$ and
$S_{\text{ram}}$ from the parameter vector (it puts each free parameter where the
specification says), and `.sem_ram_m()` builds $m$:

```{r}
#| label: ram
mats <- medfit:::.sem_ram_mats(ram, theta)
A <- mats$a
Sram <- mats$s
m <- medfit:::.sem_ram_m(ram, theta)
Fsel <- diag(ram$nv)[ram$obs_idx, , drop = FALSE]
dimnames(A) <- dimnames(Sram) <- list(ram$vars, ram$vars)
names(m) <- ram$vars
dimnames(Fsel) <- list(ram$obs, ram$vars)
cat("A (row = target, column = source)\n")
mx(A)
cat("\nS_ram\n")
mx(Sram)
cat("\nm\n")
mx(m)
cat("\nF\n")
Fsel
```

Read $A$ one row at a time. The row `mediator1` has `r f4(A["mediator1", "treatment"])`
in the `treatment` column: that is the path $a$. The row `outcome` holds
$b$ = `r f4(A["outcome", "mediator1"])` and $c'$ = `r f4(A["outcome", "treatment"])`.
Every other entry is a structural zero, a path the model does not have. In
$S_{\text{ram}}$ the diagonal is the two residual variances and the variance of
`treatment`; the off-diagonal entries are zero because the model has no
correlated errors.

Here every variable is observed, so $F$ is the identity and does nothing. It
earns its place when the model has a latent variable, which sits in $v$ but not
in the data. A mediator measured by two indicators shows it:

```{r}
#| label: latent-f
latent <- fit_sem("
  M =~ mediator1 + mediator2
  M ~ a * treatment
  outcome ~ b * M + treatment
", mediation_demo, meanstructure = TRUE)
rl <- latent@internals$ram
Fl <- diag(rl$nv)[rl$obs_idx, , drop = FALSE]
dimnames(Fl) <- list(rl$obs, rl$vars)
Fl
```

$F$ has four rows (the four observed variables) and five columns (those four plus
the latent `M`); the `M` column is all zeros. From now on we return to the
observed model, where $F = I$.

## 3. The implied mean and covariance

A fitted model is a claim about the **moments** of the observed variables: their
means $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$. We derive both from the RAM equation.

**Step 1: solve for $v$.** Move $A v$ to the left: $(I - A)v = m + e$. The matrix
$I - A$ is invertible when the model has no feedback loop. The engine gives a parameter
vector that makes it singular (or that makes the implied covariance not positive
definite) a large finite discrepancy, so the optimizer steps back from it. Write
$B = (I - A)^{-1}$, so

$$
v = B\,(m + e).
$$

**Step 2: take the expectation.** $B$ and $m$ are constants and
$\operatorname{E}(e) = 0$, so $\operatorname{E}(v) = B\,m$.

**Step 3: take the covariance.** $\operatorname{Cov}(v) = B \operatorname{Cov}(e) B^\top
= B\,S_{\text{ram}}\,B^\top$, because $\operatorname{Cov}(M x) = M \operatorname{Cov}(x) M^\top$
for a constant matrix $M$ and the constant $m$ adds nothing to a covariance.

**Step 4: select the observed variables.** The data contain only the observed rows
of $v$, which is what multiplying by $F$ does:

$$
\mu(\theta) = F\,(I - A)^{-1} m, \qquad
\Sigma(\theta) = F\,(I - A)^{-1} S_{\text{ram}} (I - A)^{-\top} F^\top .
$$

Now push the numbers through. First $B$:

```{r}
#| label: implied
B <- solve(diag(ram$nv) - A)
mx(B)
```

Column `treatment` of $B$ reads: a one-unit change in `treatment` moves `mediator1`
by $a$ = `r f4(B["mediator1", "treatment"])` and `outcome` by $a b + c'$ =
`r f4(B["outcome", "treatment"])`. That is the total effect, the sum of the indirect
path $a b$ = `r f4(A["mediator1", "treatment"] * A["outcome", "mediator1"])` and the direct
path. $B$ collects every path from one variable to another.

```{r}
#| label: implied-hand
mu <- drop(Fsel %*% B %*% m)
Sigma <- Fsel %*% B %*% Sram %*% t(B) %*% t(Fsel)
cat("mu\n")
mx(mu)
cat("\nSigma\n")
mx(Sigma)

# the engine's own helpers, and the largest absolute difference from the hand computation
c(
  mean = max(abs(medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram, theta) - mu)),
  cov = max(abs(medfit:::.sem_implied(ram, theta) - Sigma))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: implied-hand-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(max(abs(medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram, theta) - mu)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(medfit:::.sem_implied(ram, theta) - Sigma)) < 1e-10)
```

The last two numbers are the largest absolute differences between our matrix
product and the engine's helpers, so they would be large if either side had an
error. This model has as many free parameters as observed moments (Section 6 counts
them) and is identified, so it can match any sample means and covariances. Compare with
the sample moments:

```{r}
#| label: saturated
x <- as.matrix(fit@data[, ram$obs])
xbar <- colMeans(x)
S <- cov(x) * (n - 1) / n
cat("sample mean\n")
mx(xbar)
cat("\nsample covariance (divisor n)\n")
mx(S)
c(mean = max(abs(mu - xbar)), cov = max(abs(Sigma - S)))
```

```{r}
#| label: saturated-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(max(abs(mu - xbar)) < 1e-8, max(abs(Sigma - S)) < 1e-8)
```

The model reproduces the sample mean and covariance to rounding. An identified model
with as many free parameters as observed moments (zero degrees of freedom) is
**saturated**: it reproduces every data set this way, so it cannot be rejected.

## 4. The discrepancy

The engine finds $\theta$ by maximum likelihood. This section derives the
function it minimizes, including the term the mean structure adds.

**Setup.** The data are $n$ rows $x_1, \dots, x_n$, each a vector of the $p$
observed variables, assumed independent and multivariate normal with mean
$\mu$ and covariance $\Sigma$. The density of one row is

$$
f(x_i) = (2\pi)^{-p/2} |\Sigma|^{-1/2} \exp\left\{ -\tfrac12 (x_i - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x_i - \mu) \right\}.
$$

**Step 1: the log likelihood.** Rows are independent, so the log likelihood is
the sum of the log densities:

$$
-2 \log L = n p \log 2\pi + n \log|\Sigma| + \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x_i - \mu).
$$

**Step 2: split each deviation.** Write $x_i - \mu = (x_i - \bar x) + d$, with
$\bar x$ the sample mean and $d = \bar x - \mu$ the gap between the sample mean
and the model's mean. Expanding the quadratic form gives three terms:

$$
\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x_i - \bar x)
+ 2\, d^\top \Sigma^{-1} \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)
+ n\, d^\top \Sigma^{-1} d .
$$

The middle term is zero, because deviations from the sample mean sum to zero
($\sum_i (x_i - \bar x) = 0$).

**Step 3: turn the first sum into a trace.** A scalar equals its own trace, and
$\operatorname{tr}(u^\top M u) = \operatorname{tr}(M u u^\top)$, so
$\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x_i - \bar x) = \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1} \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(x_i - \bar x)^\top\bigr) = n \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} S)$,
with $S$ the sample covariance with divisor $n$ (the engine's choice, which is
the maximum likelihood estimate).

**Step 4: collect.**

$$
-2 \log L = n \left[ p \log 2\pi + \log|\Sigma| + \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} S) + d^\top \Sigma^{-1} d \right].
$$

**Step 5: scale to a discrepancy.** The engine minimizes the function that is
this bracket with the saturated value subtracted. The saturated model sets
$\mu = \bar x$ and $\Sigma = S$, giving $d = 0$ and a bracket of
$p \log 2\pi + \log|S| + \operatorname{tr}(I) = p\log 2\pi + \log|S| + p$. Subtracting it leaves

$$
F_{ML}(\theta) = \log|\Sigma| + \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} S) - \log|S| - p
+ \underbrace{(\bar x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\bar x - \mu)}_{\text{mean term}},
\qquad -2\log L = n \left( F_{ML} + \log|S| + p + p \log 2\pi \right).
$$

Two facts follow. First, $F_{ML} \ge 0$, with equality exactly when the model
reproduces the sample mean and covariance (a saturated model always does). The
proof is short. The mean term is a quadratic form in a positive definite matrix, so
it is nonnegative. For the rest, let $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_p$ be the eigenvalues
of $\Sigma^{-1} S$, all positive because $S$ is positive definite (the engine requires it).
$\Sigma^{-1} S$ is similar to the symmetric matrix $\Sigma^{-1/2} S \Sigma^{-1/2}$, so all
$\lambda_j = 1$ means $\Sigma = S$. Then $\log|\Sigma| - \log|S| = -\sum_j \log\lambda_j$ and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} S) = \sum_j \lambda_j$, so the covariance part equals
$\sum_j (\lambda_j - \log \lambda_j - 1)$. Each term is nonnegative, because
$\log \lambda \le \lambda - 1$, and it is zero only at $\lambda = 1$. Second,
$n F_{ML}$ is the likelihood-ratio statistic against the saturated model, since the
saturated model's $-2\log L$ is the bracket with $F_{ML} = 0$; that is why it is the
model chi-square. Without a mean structure the means are free,
$d = 0$, and the mean term is absent: that is the whole of the extension.

**Worked instance.** Our free model is saturated, so $F_{ML} = 0$ and there is
nothing to see. Fix the outcome's intercept at zero with `outcome ~ 0*1` and the
model can no longer match the outcome mean. Section 6 returns to what the
restriction means; for now it gives a nonzero $F_{ML}$ to take apart.

```{r}
#| label: restricted
syntax0 <- sub("outcome ~ 1", "outcome ~ 0*1", syntax, fixed = TRUE)
fit0 <- fit_sem(syntax0, mediation_demo)
ram0 <- fit0@internals$ram
th0 <- fit0@theta
Sigma0 <- medfit:::.sem_implied(ram0, th0)
mu0 <- medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram0, th0)
d <- xbar - mu0
Sinv <- solve(Sigma0)
p <- length(xbar)

cov_part <- log(det(Sigma0)) + sum(diag(Sinv %*% S)) - log(det(S)) - p
mean_part <- drop(t(d) %*% Sinv %*% d)
c(covariance = cov_part, mean = mean_part, total = cov_part + mean_part, engine = fit0@f)
```

```{r}
#| label: restricted-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(abs(cov_part + mean_part - fit0@f) < 1e-10, cov_part > 0, mean_part > 0)
```

The gap vector $d = \bar x - \mu$ shows where the restriction bites:

```{r}
#| label: gap
mx(d)
```

The model matches the sample means of `mediator1` and `treatment` (their intercepts
are free) and misses the outcome mean by `r f3(d["outcome"])`. Both parts of the
discrepancy are positive, which is worth a moment. The paths $b$ and $c'$ appear in
the covariance and in the outcome mean at once, so the optimizer moves them away from
the values that match the covariance exactly (compare $b$ = `r f4(coef(fit0)["b"])` here
with `r f4(coef(fit)["b"])` in the free fit) to close part of the mean gap, and pays
for it in the covariance part. The two terms trade off; their sum is what is minimized.

The log likelihood follows from the same pieces. Summing the log density row by
row, with no shortcut, must agree with `logLik()`, which uses the formula in
step 5:

```{r}
#| label: loglik
ll_rows <- sum(vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  di <- x[i, ] - mu0
  -0.5 * (p * log(2 * pi) + log(det(Sigma0)) + drop(t(di) %*% Sinv %*% di))
}, numeric(1)))
ll_formula <- -0.5 * n * (fit0@f + log(det(S)) + p + p * log(2 * pi))
c(row_by_row = ll_rows, formula = ll_formula, logLik = as.numeric(logLik(fit0)))
```

```{r}
#| label: loglik-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(abs(ll_rows - ll_formula) < 1e-6, abs(ll_rows - as.numeric(logLik(fit0))) < 1e-6)
```

## 5. The gradient

The optimizer needs $\partial F_{ML} / \partial \theta_k$. The engine supplies it
analytically. This section derives it in four steps, and then checks each factor
against finite differences.

**Step 1: the matrix calculus.** For a symmetric positive definite $\Sigma$,
$\partial \log|\Sigma| = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} \partial\Sigma)$ and
$\partial \Sigma^{-1} = -\Sigma^{-1} (\partial\Sigma) \Sigma^{-1}$. The first is
Jacobi's formula; the second follows from differentiating $\Sigma\Sigma^{-1} = I$. By
the cyclic property of the trace, $d^\top \Sigma^{-1} d = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} d d^\top)$,
so the mean term can be treated as a trace too. Write
$S_{\text{eff}} = S + d d^\top$, so that holding $d$ fixed,

$$
\partial F_{ML} = \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1} \partial\Sigma\bigr)
- \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1} S_{\text{eff}} \Sigma^{-1} \partial\Sigma\bigr)
+ (\text{change through } d).
$$

**Step 2: the change through $d$.** $d = \bar x - \mu$, so $\partial d = -\partial\mu$
(the sample mean does not depend on $\theta$) and
$\partial (d^\top \Sigma^{-1} d)|_{\Sigma\ \text{fixed}} = -2\, (\partial\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} d$.
Together:

$$
\frac{\partial F_{ML}}{\partial \theta_k}
= \operatorname{tr}\bigl(W\, \partial_k \Sigma\bigr) - 2\, (\partial_k \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} d,
\qquad W = \Sigma^{-1} - \Sigma^{-1} S_{\text{eff}} \Sigma^{-1}.
$$

**Step 3: the derivative of $B$.** To get $\partial_k\Sigma$ and $\partial_k\mu$ we need
how $B = (I - A)^{-1}$ moves. Differentiate $B (I - A) = I$:
$(\partial B)(I - A) - B\,\partial A = 0$, so $\partial B = B\,(\partial A)\,B$.

**Step 4: the derivative of the moments.** Let $e_r$ be the $r$th unit vector.

- A path entry $A_{r c}$ has $\partial A = e_r e_c^\top$, hence $\partial B = B e_r e_c^\top B$.
  Then $\partial \mu = F B e_r \,(B m)_c$ and
  $\partial \Sigma_{\text{full}} = B e_r e_c^\top B\, S_{\text{ram}} B^\top + \text{its transpose}$,
  where $\Sigma_{\text{full}} = B S_{\text{ram}} B^\top$ is the covariance of all of $v$.
- An intercept $m_j$ moves $\mu$ by $F B e_j$ and does not touch $\Sigma$.
- A variance or covariance entry $(S_{\text{ram}})_{r c}$ has
  $\partial \Sigma_{\text{full}} = B e_r e_c^\top B^\top$ (plus its transpose when $r \neq c$,
  because the matrix is symmetric and the two entries are one parameter) and does not touch $\mu$.

Two parameters with the same label are one parameter, so their contributions add.
The engine's `.sem_dsigma()` and `.sem_dmu()` return these derivatives; we check
them against central differences of `.sem_implied()` and `.sem_implied_mean()`,
which know nothing about the algebra above:

```{r}
#| label: deriv-check
central <- function(f, theta, k, h = 1e-6) {
  up <- dn <- theta
  up[k] <- theta[k] + h
  dn[k] <- theta[k] - h
  (f(up) - f(dn)) / (2 * h)
}
dsig <- medfit:::.sem_dsigma(th0, ram0)
dmu <- medfit:::.sem_dmu(th0, ram0)
err_sigma <- vapply(seq_along(th0), function(k) {
  max(abs(dsig[[k]] - central(function(t) medfit:::.sem_implied(ram0, t), th0, k)))
}, numeric(1))
err_mu <- vapply(seq_along(th0), function(k) {
  max(abs(dmu[, k] - central(function(t) medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram0, t), th0, k)))
}, numeric(1))
signif(cbind(sigma = err_sigma, mu = err_mu), 2) |> `rownames<-`(names(th0))
```

```{r}
#| label: deriv-check-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(max(err_sigma, err_mu) < 1e-6)
```

Each row is a free parameter and each entry is the largest absolute discrepancy
between the analytic derivative and the finite difference, so a wrong derivative
would show as a number near the size of the derivative itself. Now the
whole gradient. At the optimum it must vanish. At another point it must match a
finite difference of $F_{ML}$ itself, so we test it at the engine's starting
value, where the gradient is large:

```{r}
#| label: grad-check
smp <- medfit:::.sem_sample(fit0@data, ram0)
grad_formula <- function(theta) {
  Sg <- medfit:::.sem_implied(ram0, theta)
  mug <- medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram0, theta)
  Si <- solve(Sg)
  dg <- smp$xbar - mug
  W <- Si - Si %*% (smp$s + tcrossprod(dg)) %*% Si
  ds <- medfit:::.sem_dsigma(theta, ram0)
  dm <- medfit:::.sem_dmu(theta, ram0)
  vapply(seq_along(theta), function(k) {
    sum(W * ds[[k]]) - 2 * drop(crossprod(dm[, k], Si %*% dg))
  }, numeric(1))
}
start <- medfit:::.sem_default_start(ram0, smp)
fml <- function(t) medfit:::.sem_fml(t, ram0, smp)
fd <- vapply(seq_along(start), function(k) central(fml, start, k), numeric(1))
signif(cbind(
  formula = grad_formula(start),
  finite_difference = fd,
  engine = medfit:::.sem_grad(start, ram0, smp)
), 4) |> `rownames<-`(names(start))
```

```{r}
#| label: grad-optimum
c(at_start_vs_fd = max(abs(grad_formula(start) - fd)),
  at_optimum = max(abs(grad_formula(th0))))
```

```{r}
#| label: grad-optimum-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(max(abs(grad_formula(start) - fd)) < 1e-6, max(abs(grad_formula(th0))) < 1e-6,
          max(abs(grad_formula(start)[names(start) %in% c("mediator1~1", "treatment~1")])) < 1e-12)
```

The three columns agree. The last two rows, the intercepts of `mediator1` and
`treatment`, are zero for a reason worth seeing. The default start sets these two
intercepts so that the implied means of `mediator1` and `treatment` equal their sample
means, which leaves a gap only in the outcome: $d = d_y e_y$. With every variable
observed, $\Sigma^{-1} = (I - A)^\top S_{\text{ram}}^{-1} (I - A)$. The outcome causes
nothing, so $(I - A) e_y = e_y$, and its residual is uncorrelated with the others, so
$S_{\text{ram}}^{-1} e_y = e_y / s_y$ with $s_y$ its residual variance. Hence
$\Sigma^{-1} d = (d_y / s_y)(I - A)^\top e_y$, and the gradient of intercept $m_j$, which is
$-2\,(B e_j)^\top \Sigma^{-1} d$ by Step 2 and Step 4, equals
$-2\,(d_y / s_y)\, e_j^\top B^\top (I - A)^\top e_y = -2\,(d_y/s_y)\, e_j^\top e_y = 0$ for every
$j$ other than the outcome. At the optimum every component of the gradient is
numerically zero: the fit sits at a stationary point.

## 6. Counting moments and degrees of freedom

The data summarize to $p$ means and $p(p+1)/2$ distinct variances and covariances,
so a model with a mean structure faces $p(p+3)/2$ **observed moments**. Here
$p = 3$ gives `r medfit:::.sem_moments(ram)` moments. The **degrees of freedom**
are the moments minus the free parameters,

$$
\text{df} = \frac{p(p+1)}{2} + p - q ,
$$

with $q$ the number of free parameters after equality constraints (Chapter 3). The
free model has $q$ = `r ram$q`, so df = `r fit@df`: saturated, as Section 3 found.
Fixing the outcome intercept removes one parameter and no moment:

```{r}
#| label: df
data.frame(
  model = c("all intercepts free", "outcome ~ 0*1"),
  moments = c(medfit:::.sem_moments(ram), medfit:::.sem_moments(ram0)),
  free_parameters = c(ram$q, ram0$q),
  df = c(fit@df, fit0@df),
  chisq = round(c(n * fit@f, n * fit0@f), 4)
)
```

So `y ~ 0*1` is a one-degree-of-freedom **restriction**, and its chi-square is
$n F_{ML}$ = `r f3(n * fit0@f)`, the number Section 4 took apart. What does it
test? With the outcome intercept at zero, the outcome mean is no longer free: the
RAM equation forces $\mu_y = b\,\mu_{m} + c'\,\mu_x$, the mean carried by the
mediator and the treatment through the paths. The data can contradict that, and
the restriction asks whether they do. `anova()`, the subject of Chapter 5, turns the
same quantity into a p-value:

```{r}
#| label: anova
anova(fit0, fit)
```

A Wald test of the same hypothesis reads the free fit's intercept and its standard
error, $z = \hat m_y / \operatorname{SE}(\hat m_y)$:

```{r}
#| label: wald
est <- theta["outcome~1"]
se <- sqrt(diag(fit@vcov))["outcome~1"]
c(intercept = unname(est), se = unname(se), wald_chisq = unname((est / se)^2),
  lr_chisq = n * fit0@f)
```

The Wald and likelihood-ratio statistics are two standard ways to test one
parameter. They agree in large samples and differ in finite ones: here
`r f3((est / se)^2)` against `r f3(n * fit0@f)`.

## 7. Cross-checks: lavaan and OpenMx

Both packages fit the restricted model to the same data. lavaan reports the
chi-square, the degrees of freedom and the log likelihood directly. We set
`meanstructure = TRUE` and `fixed.x = FALSE` so that it estimates the exogenous
mean and variance the way the native engine does (Chapter 4 explains the
alternative).

```{r}
#| label: lavaan
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)
lv <- lavaan::sem("
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment
  outcome ~ 0 * 1
", data = mediation_demo, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed.x = FALSE)
est_lv <- lavaan::coef(lv)
est_mf <- coef(fit0)
common <- intersect(names(est_lv), names(est_mf))
data.frame(
  quantity = c("chisq", "df", "logLik"),
  medfit = c(n * fit0@f, fit0@df, as.numeric(logLik(fit0))),
  lavaan = c(lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "chisq"), lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "df"),
             lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "logl"))
)
c(coefficients_compared = length(common),
  largest_absolute_difference = max(abs(est_lv[common] - est_mf[common])))
```

```{r}
#| label: lavaan-check
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("lavaan", quietly = TRUE)
stopifnot(abs(n * fit0@f - lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "chisq")) < 1e-6,
          abs(as.numeric(logLik(fit0)) - lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "logl")) < 1e-6,
          max(abs(est_lv[common] - est_mf[common])) < 1e-6)
```

The second result is the largest absolute difference over the coefficients the two
fits share.

OpenMx fits the same model on the raw data. Its RAM interface mirrors the matrices of Section 2: `mxPath` with
`arrows = 1` fills $A$, `arrows = 2` fills $S_{\text{ram}}$, and a path from
`"one"` fills $m$. The outcome's intercept path is fixed at 0.

```{r}
#| label: openmx
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("OpenMx", quietly = TRUE)
suppressMessages(library(OpenMx))
mxOption(NULL, "Number of Threads", 1)
dat <- mediation_demo[, c("mediator1", "treatment", "outcome")]
vars <- names(dat)
mod <- mxModel(
  "restricted", type = "RAM", manifestVars = vars,
  mxPath(from = "treatment", to = "mediator1", values = 0.4, labels = "a"),
  mxPath(from = c("mediator1", "treatment"), to = "outcome", values = 0.5, labels = c("b", "cp")),
  mxPath(from = vars, arrows = 2, values = 1, labels = paste0("v_", vars)),
  mxPath(from = "one", to = c("mediator1", "treatment"), values = 0, labels = c("m_m", "m_t")),
  mxPath(from = "one", to = "outcome", free = FALSE, values = 0),
  mxData(dat, type = "raw")
)
run <- mxRun(mod, silent = TRUE)
smry <- summary(run)
est_mx <- stats::setNames(smry$parameters$Estimate, smry$parameters$name)
mx_map <- c(a = "a", b = "b", cp = "cp", "mediator1~~mediator1" = "v_mediator1",
            "outcome~~outcome" = "v_outcome", "treatment~~treatment" = "v_treatment",
            "mediator1~1" = "m_m", "treatment~1" = "m_t")
data.frame(quantity = "-2 log L", medfit = -2 * as.numeric(logLik(fit0)),
           OpenMx = smry$Minus2LogLikelihood)
c(largest_absolute_difference = max(abs(est_mx[mx_map] - est_mf[names(mx_map)])))
c(OpenMx_degreesOfFreedom = smry$degreesOfFreedom, data_values_n_times_p = n * p,
  free_parameters = nrow(smry$parameters), saturated_moments = medfit:::.sem_moments(ram0),
  medfit_df = fit0@df)
```

```{r}
#| label: openmx-check
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("OpenMx", quietly = TRUE)
stopifnot(abs(-2 * as.numeric(logLik(fit0)) - smry$Minus2LogLikelihood) < 1e-3,
          smry$degreesOfFreedom == n * p - nrow(smry$parameters),
          medfit:::.sem_moments(ram0) - nrow(smry$parameters) == fit0@df)
```

The two `-2 log L` values agree; the coefficients agree less closely than lavaan's,
a difference in where the two optimizers stop.

The last line shows that OpenMx's `degreesOfFreedom` is a different count. For raw
data OpenMx subtracts the number of free parameters from the number of observed data
values, $n p$. The chi-square degrees of freedom compare against the saturated model,
which has $p(p+3)/2$ parameters, so they are the saturated moments minus the free
parameters, the engine's `fit0@df`.

## 8. The information is a sum

One more consequence of the mean structure, used in Chapter 5. The **score** of
one row is the gradient of its log density with respect to $\theta$. The
**expected information** of $n$ independent rows is $n$ times the covariance matrix
of one row's score (its definition; for a likelihood regular enough to differentiate
under the integral it also equals the expected negative Hessian, Chapter 5). Under
normality it is the sum of a covariance part and a mean part with no cross term:

$$
I_{kl} = \frac{n}{2} \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1} \partial_k\Sigma\, \Sigma^{-1} \partial_l\Sigma\bigr)
+ n\, (\partial_k \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\partial_l \mu).
$$

Why. Write $u = x_i - \mu$, so $u \sim N(0, \Sigma)$. Differentiating the log density
$-\tfrac12\bigl[\log|\Sigma| + u^\top \Sigma^{-1} u\bigr]$ (the same calculus as Section 5, with
$\partial u = -\partial\mu$) gives the score of one row in two parts,

$$
s_k = \underbrace{(\partial_k\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} u}_{\text{mean part, linear in } u}
+ \underbrace{\tfrac12\bigl[u^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\partial_k\Sigma)\, \Sigma^{-1} u - \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma)\bigr]}_{\text{covariance part, quadratic in } u}.
$$

Cross term: the covariance of a linear and a quadratic function of $u$ involves
third-order moments of $u$, which are zero because the normal distribution is
symmetric about its mean. Mean part: $\operatorname{Cov}\bigl((\partial_k\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} u,\,
(\partial_l\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} u\bigr) = (\partial_k\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\partial_l\mu)$, since
$\operatorname{Cov}(u) = \Sigma$. Covariance part: for symmetric $M, N$, the normal moment identity
$\operatorname{Cov}(u^\top M u,\, u^\top N u) = 2\operatorname{tr}(M\Sigma N\Sigma)$ with
$M = \tfrac12\Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}$ and $N = \tfrac12\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}$ gives
$\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma)$. Multiplying by $n$ gives the
two terms above. Check the result against the engine, which computes the same two terms:

```{r}
#| label: info-sum
sigma_inv <- solve(Sigma0)
cov_info <- 0.5 * n * outer(seq_along(th0), seq_along(th0), Vectorize(function(k, l) {
  sum(diag(sigma_inv %*% dsig[[k]] %*% sigma_inv %*% dsig[[l]]))
}))
mean_info <- n * crossprod(dmu, sigma_inv %*% dmu)
info_hand <- cov_info + mean_info
info_engine <- medfit:::.sem_info_expected(th0, ram0, smp, NULL)
c(difference = max(abs(info_hand - info_engine)), largest_entry = max(abs(info_engine)))
```

```{r}
#| label: info-sum-check
#| include: false
stopifnot(max(abs(info_hand - info_engine)) < 1e-8 * max(abs(info_engine)))
```

The hand-built information matches the engine's. Its inverse estimates the covariance
matrix of the estimates; the engine's default uses the observed information instead
(Chapter 5 compares the two), and Chapter 2 shows why the inverse needs a change of
coordinates when the means are large.

## Check yourself

1. In the RAM form, which matrix would you change to add a correlation between two
   residuals? Which to add a path from the treatment to a new mediator?
   (Answer: $S_{\text{ram}}$, then $A$.)
2. A model with $p = 4$ observed variables, a mean structure and 12 free
   parameters has how many degrees of freedom? (Answer: $4 \cdot 5 / 2 + 4 - 12 = 2$.)
3. Why is the middle term in Step 2 of Section 4 zero, and what would break if
   $\bar x$ were replaced by some other center? (Answer: deviations from the
   sample mean sum to zero; for another center the cross term would not vanish and
   the likelihood would not split into a covariance part and a mean part.)

**The default since 0.15.0.** An unset `meanstructure` is `TRUE`, so every native fit has the saturated mean part of
this chapter, not only a fit whose syntax writes a `~1` row or a product term; an unset `fixed_x` fixes the exogenous
observed variables (Chapter 4). The setup chunk of each chapter defines a `fit_sem()` wrapper that pins the 0.14.x
settings (`fixed_x = FALSE, meanstructure = NULL`), so the matrices here are the joint, covariance-first ones. Section 4
is why the paths, variances and their standard errors do not change under the default. What does change (the
parameter count, `logLik()`, AIC and BIC, the names in `coef()`) is on the live example in Section 6 of
[Chapter 4](04-fixed-x.qmd) and in
[Native defaults in 0.15.0](https://data-wise.github.io/medfit/articles/native-defaults-0-15.html).
